marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q001.takeaway: Ovaries secrete estrogen, progesterone and inhibin; gonadotropins are secreted by anterior pituitary gonadotrophs.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q001.displayText:
Ovaries secrete estrogen, progesterone and inhibin; gonadotropins are secreted by anterior pituitary gonadotrophs.

Gonadotropins (FSH, LH) are not secreted by the ovary. They are secreted by the anterior

pituitary.

Ovaries secrete estrogen, progesterone, and inhibin B.
emphasis: Ovaries secrete estrogen, progesterone and inhibin; gonadotropins are secreted by anterior pituitary gonadotrophs

rationales.b: Progesterone is produced by corpus luteum and, in pregnancy, placenta.
rationales.d: Inhibin B is secreted by ovarian granulosa cells.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q002.takeaway: Ovulation usually occurs about 14 days before the next menstruation because the luteal phase is relatively constant.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q002.displayText:
Ovulation usually occurs about 14 days before the next menstruation because the luteal phase is relatively constant.

Ovulation occurs 14 days before menses, regardless of cycle length.

If we calculate the day of menstruation from the beginning of the cycle, in a 28-day cycle,

ovulation occurs on day 14 and in a 35-day cycle, ovulation will occur on day 22.

Option B: LH surge leads to ovulation. Ovulation does not occur before LH surge.
Option C: The ruptured ovarian follicle (after ovulation) is converted into corpus luteum.
Ovulation does not occur after corpus luteal maturation.
Option D: Ovulation will occur 14 days before menstruation, i.e. on day 22 of a 35-day cycle. It
does not occur 22 days before menstruation.
emphasis: Ovulation usually occurs about 14 days before the next menstruation because the luteal phase is relatively constant

rationales.b: Ovulation precedes the LH surge; the LH surge triggers ovulation rather than following it.
rationales.d: A 22-day interval before menses is longer than the usual luteal-phase timing.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q003.takeaway: The corpus luteum begins regression about 10 days after ovulation if pregnancy has not rescued it.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q003.displayText:
The corpus luteum begins regression about 10 days after ovulation if pregnancy has not rescued it.

The human corpus luteum starts regressing ~10 days after ovulation.

Ovulation occurs on day 14, and the day corpus luteum begins to regress on day 25 of the menstrual cycle.

Therefore,
Days after ovulation when corpus luteum starts regressing = 25 - 14 = 11 days.

The human corpus luteum is programmed to live for 14 days, plus or minus 2 days (corpus luteum of menstruation).
emphasis: The corpus luteum begins regression about 10 days after ovulation if pregnancy has not rescued it

rationales.a: Five days is generally too early for luteal regression.
rationales.c: Twenty-four days post-ovulation is far beyond the expected start of regression.
rationales.d: Seventeen days is later than the typical regression onset.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q004.takeaway: Humans have menstrual, ovarian and endometrial cycles; the estrous cycle is characteristic of many non-primate mammals.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q004.displayText:
Humans have menstrual, ovarian and endometrial cycles; the estrous cycle is characteristic of many non-primate mammals.

Estrous cycle is not seen in humans.
Mammals other than primates do not menstruate, and their sexual cycle is called an estrous cycle.
It is named for the conspicuous period of “heat” (estrus) at the time of ovulation, normally the
only time during which the sexual interest of the female is aroused.

In spontaneously ovulating species with estrous cycles, such as the rat, no episodic vaginal
bleeding occurs, but the underlying endocrine events are essentially the same as those in the
menstrual cycle.
In other species, ovulation is induced by copulation (reflex ovulation).
emphasis: Humans have menstrual, ovarian and endometrial cycles; the estrous cycle is characteristic of many non-primate mammals

rationales.b: Menstruation is the defining feature of the human reproductive cycle.
rationales.c: Endometrial changes occur cyclically in humans.
rationales.d: Ovarian follicular/luteal phases occur in humans.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q005.takeaway: Progesterone from the corpus luteum dominates the post-ovulatory luteal phase.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q005.displayText:
Progesterone from the corpus luteum dominates the post-ovulatory luteal phase.

• Progesterone is the dominant hormone during the luteal phase.
• The corpus luteum in the non-pregnant woman secretes large quantities of progesterone and a small amount of estrogen, as well as inhibin.
• In terms of ovarian function, the menstrual cycle may be divided into two phases approximately equal in length and separated by ovulation.
• The follicular phase, during which a mature follicle and secondary oocyte develop; and
• The luteal phase begins after ovulation and lasts until the death of the corpus luteum.

Follicular phase (days 0–14)
• A primordial follicle develops to the Graafian stage, with atresia of neighboring follicles.
• LH and FSH receptors are up-regulated in theca and granulosa cells.
• Estradiol levels increase and cause proliferation of the uterus.
• FSH and LH levels are suppressed by the negative feedback effect of estradiol on the anterior pituitary.
• Progesterone levels are low.

Ovulation (day 14)
• Occurs 14 days before menses, regardless of cycle length. Thus, in a 28-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 14; in a 35-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 22.
• A burst of estradiol synthesis at the end of the follicular phase has a positive feedback effect on the secretion of FSH and LH (LH surge).
• Ovulation occurs as a result of the estrogen-induced LH surge.
• Estrogen levels decrease just after ovulation (but rise again during the luteal phase).
• Cervical mucus increases in quantity; it becomes less viscous and more penetrable by sperm.

Luteal phase (days 14–28)
• The corpus luteum begins to develop, and it synthesizes estrogen and progesterone. Vascularity and secretory activity of the endometrium increase to prepare for receipt of a fertilized egg.
• Basal body temperature increases because of the effect of progesterone on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center.
• If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses at the end of the luteal phase. As a result, estradiol and progesterone levels decrease abruptly.

Menses (days 0–4)
• The endometrium is sloughed because of the abrupt withdrawal of estradiol and progesterone.
emphasis: Progesterone from the corpus luteum dominates the post-ovulatory luteal phase

rationales.a: Estrogen rises before ovulation and is present in luteal phase, but progesterone predominates after ovulation.
rationales.c: Prolactin is not the dominant ovarian luteal hormone.
rationales.d: Oxytocin is not the dominant luteal steroid.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q006.takeaway: Progesterone converts and maintains the endometrium in the secretory phase after ovulation.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q006.displayText:
Progesterone converts and maintains the endometrium in the secretory phase after ovulation.

Progesterone is mainly responsible for the maintenance of endometrial thickness in the post-ovulatory phase.

The menstrual cycle consists of three phases: the menstrual phase, the proliferative phase, and the secretory, or progestational, phase.

Menstrual phase: This phase is characterized by the discharge of blood and endometrial debris from the vagina.
• It coincides with the end of the ovarian luteal phase and onset of a new follicular phase.
• Withdrawal of progesterone on the degeneration of the corpus luteum (CL) leads simultaneously to sloughing of the endometrium (menstruation) and development of new follicles in the ovary under the influence of rising gonadotropic hormone levels.

Proliferative Phase: Thus, menstrual flow ceases, and the proliferative phase of the uterine cycle begins concurrently with the last portion of the ovarian follicular phase.
• When the menstrual flow ceases, a thin endometrial layer less than 1-mm thick remains. Estrogen stimulates proliferation of epithelial cells, glands, and blood vessels in the endometrium, increasing this lining to a thickness of 3 to 5 mm.
• The estrogen-dominant proliferative phase lasts from the end of menstruation to ovulation. Peak estrogen levels trigger the luteinizing hormone (LH) surge responsible for ovulation.

Secretory or Progestational Phase: After ovulation, when a new corpus luteum is formed, the uterus enters the secretory, or progestational, phase, which coincides in time with the ovarian luteal phase. The corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone and estrogen. Progesterone converts the thickened, estrogen-primed endometrium to a richly vascularized, glycogen-filled tissue.
• This period is called either the secretory phase, because the endometrial glands are actively secreting glycogen into the uterine lumen for early nourishment of a developing embryo before it implants, or the progestational (“before pregnancy”) phase, referring to the development of a lush endometrial lining capable of supporting an early embryo after implantation.
• If fertilization and implantation do not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates and a new follicular phase and menstrual phase begin again.
emphasis: Progesterone converts and maintains the endometrium in the secretory phase after ovulation

rationales.a: Estrogen mainly drives proliferative thickening before ovulation.
rationales.c: LH supports corpus-luteum function but is not the direct hormone maintaining endometrial thickness.
rationales.d: FSH stimulates follicular development rather than postovulatory endometrium.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q007.takeaway: Home ovulation kits detect the urinary LH surge that precedes ovulation.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q007.displayText:
Home ovulation kits detect the urinary LH surge that precedes ovulation.

Detection of an increased LH level in urine will be performed by this ovulation predictor kit.

The most important physiological marker of imminent ovulation is luteinizing hormone (LH) surge, which is characterized by an increased level of LH in serum and urine. A peak level of 75 ng/mL of LH in serum is required for ovulation. LH surge occurs 24–36 hours before ovulation. LH peak lasts 24 hours.

LH surge causes the following:
• Completion of meiosis of ovum
• Ovulation
• Development of corpus luteum
emphasis: Home ovulation kits detect the urinary LH surge that precedes ovulation

rationales.a: Estrogen rises before ovulation but is not the hormone measured by standard LH predictor kits.
rationales.b: Prolactin does not trigger ovulation and is not the kit target.
rationales.c: hCG is detected in pregnancy tests, not ordinary ovulation kits.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q008.takeaway: Sustained high estrogen with low progesterone late in the follicular phase generates positive feedback and the LH surge.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q008.displayText:
Sustained high estrogen with low progesterone late in the follicular phase generates positive feedback and the LH surge.

Positive feedback action of estrogen for inducing luteinizing hormone (LH) surge is associated with high estrogen: low progesterone.
emphasis: Sustained high estrogen with low progesterone late in the follicular phase generates positive feedback and the LH surge

rationales.b: Low estrogen cannot provide the sustained estrogen-positive feedback required.
rationales.c: High progesterone tends to inhibit gonadotropin surge rather than support it.
rationales.d: Low estrogen and low progesterone do not produce the preovulatory positive feedback.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q009.takeaway: Sustained high estradiol from the dominant follicle switches feedback to positive and triggers the preovulatory LH surge.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q009.displayText:
Sustained high estradiol from the dominant follicle switches feedback to positive and triggers the preovulatory LH surge.

Increased luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion just before ovulation is due to positive feedback by estrogen.
emphasis: Sustained high estradiol from the dominant follicle switches feedback to positive and triggers the preovulatory LH surge

rationales.a: Progesterone is not the principal positive-feedback trigger before ovulation.
rationales.c: FSH does not positively feed back to cause the LH surge.
rationales.d: Relaxin is not the ovulatory surge signal.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q010.takeaway: Placental hCG rescues the corpus luteum in early pregnancy until placental steroid production is established.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q010.displayText:
Placental hCG rescues the corpus luteum in early pregnancy until placental steroid production is established.

Human chorionic gonadotrophin (HCG) causes persistence of the corpus luteum and prevents menstruation in pregnancy.

The fate of the corpus luteum
• If the ovum is not fertilized, about 2 days before the end of the monthly cycle, the corpus luteum in the ovary involutes.
• If fertilization occurs, under the influence of human chorionic gonadotropin, the corpus luteum in the mother's ovary grows to about twice its initial size by a month or so after pregnancy begins.
• The corpus luteum secretes estrogens and progesterone and maintains the decidual nature of the uterine endometrium, which is necessary for the early development of the fetus.
• The corpus luteum of pregnancy involutes slowly after the 13th to 17th week of gestation. After that time, the placenta secretes sufficient quantities of progesterone and estrogens to maintain pregnancy for the remainder of the gestation period.
emphasis: Placental hCG rescues the corpus luteum in early pregnancy until placental steroid production is established

rationales.a: Estrogen alone does not rescue the early corpus luteum.
rationales.b: Progesterone is produced by the corpus luteum but does not provide the embryonic rescue signal.
rationales.c: Oxytocin has no role in maintaining the early corpus luteum.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q011.takeaway: FSH receptors are on granulosa cells, where FSH promotes follicular growth and aromatase activity.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q011.displayText:
FSH receptors are on granulosa cells, where FSH promotes follicular growth and aromatase activity.

• Granulosa cells express the FSH receptor.
• Theca interna cells express LH receptor.

Theca interna cells have many LH receptors. LH acts via cAMP to increase conversion of cholesterol to androstenedione. The theca interna cells supply androstenedione to the granulosa cells. The granulosa cells make estradiol when provided with androgens.

Granulosa cells have many FSH receptors. FSH facilitates their secretion of estradiol by acting via cAMP to increase their aromatase activity. Mature granulosa cells also acquire LH receptors, and LH also stimulates estradiol production.
emphasis: FSH receptors are on granulosa cells, where FSH promotes follicular growth and aromatase activity

rationales.a: Theca cells primarily express LH receptors and synthesize androgen precursors.
rationales.c: Leydig cells are male testicular interstitial cells.
rationales.d: Basement membrane is structural, not a hormone-responsive cell.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q012.takeaway: Progesterone raises the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point, causing the mid-luteal basal temperature rise.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q012.displayText:
Progesterone raises the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point, causing the mid-luteal basal temperature rise.

An increase in basal body temperature in the mid-luteal phase is due to the effect of progesterone on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory centre.

Immediately after ovulation, corpus luteum is formed, which secretes progesterone in preparation of the body for potential pregnancy during that cycle. This progesterone acts on the hypothalamus and increases basal body temperature. Charting the daily basal body temperature will show an increase of approximately 0.5 to 1 degrees Fahrenheit shortly after ovulation.

Since the rise in basal body temperature coincides with ovulation, abstaining from sexual intercourse until at least 3 days after the woman's temperature has risen above her regular temperature significantly lowers the chance of pregnancy. Alternatively, using barrier methods (e.g. condom, diaphragm) during this time will prevent pregnancy.

However several factors (e.g. fever, sleep deprivation etc.) that change the basal body temperature can affect the efficacy and reliability of this method.
emphasis: Progesterone raises the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point, causing the mid-luteal basal temperature rise

rationales.a: The FSH peak is not responsible for the sustained luteal temperature increase.
rationales.b: The LH surge precedes ovulation and does not explain the mid-luteal temperature plateau.
rationales.c: Estradiol tends to have a different/less warming effect; progesterone produces the postovulatory rise.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q013.takeaway: A mid-luteal progesterone level is used to confirm that ovulation and corpus-luteum formation occurred.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q013.displayText:
A mid-luteal progesterone level is used to confirm that ovulation and corpus-luteum formation occurred.

Whether her cycle was ovulatory or not can be validly assessed by the reported serum level of progesterone.

Day 20 usually corresponds to the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. In case of anovulatory cycles, no corpus luteum will be formed and so progesterone levels will be low. Hence progesterone levels are valuable to predict if the cycles were ovulatory or not.
emphasis: A mid-luteal progesterone level is used to confirm that ovulation and corpus-luteum formation occurred

rationales.a: FSH does not provide a specific mid-luteal confirmation of ovulation.
rationales.b: LH surge predicts ovulation but a day-20 LH level does not confirm luteal progesterone production.
rationales.c: Estradiol fluctuates and is less specific than luteal progesterone for confirming ovulation.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q014.takeaway: Estradiol secretion peaks in the late follicular phase immediately before ovulation.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q014.displayText:
Estradiol secretion peaks in the late follicular phase immediately before ovulation.

• Estrogen comes from the ovary and two peaks of secretion occur, one just before ovulation and one during the mid-luteal phase.
• After menopause, estrogen secretion declines to low levels.
emphasis: Estradiol secretion peaks in the late follicular phase immediately before ovulation

rationales.a: Menopause follows ovarian follicle depletion and low estrogen.
rationales.b: Puberty is a developmental period, not the peak cyclic estradiol phase.
rationales.c: Estrogen is relatively low at menstruation compared with the preovulatory peak.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q015.takeaway: Estrogen contributes negative feedback on FSH and LH during the luteal phase, together with progesterone and inhibin.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q015.displayText:
Estrogen contributes negative feedback on FSH and LH during the luteal phase, together with progesterone and inhibin.

Estrogen inhibits FSH and LH secretion in the luteal phase.

Feedback regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis
Luteal phase: the corpus luteum secretes large quantities of progesterone and estrogen. They exert a negative feedback effect on the anterior pituitary gland causing the suppression of both FSH and LH secretion.

Preovulatory period: The high level of estrogens at this time (or the beginning of progesterone secretion by the follicles) causes a positive feedback stimulatory effect on the anterior pituitary leading to a surge of LH and to a lesser extent, FSH.

Follicular phase: secretion of estrogen and progesterone from the corpus luteum decreases, which leads to loss of negative feedback effect of these hormones on the anterior pituitary. Therefore, pituitary secretion of FSH begins to increase again, as much as twofold. LH secretion increases slightly as well.

GnRH stimulates FSH and LH secretion. Growth hormone and IGF may cause an increase in FSH and LH levels.
emphasis: Estrogen contributes negative feedback on FSH and LH during the luteal phase, together with progesterone and inhibin

rationales.a: GH is not the principal ovarian-axis negative-feedback steroid.
rationales.b: GnRH stimulates LH/FSH release rather than inhibiting them.
rationales.d: IGF-1 supports ovarian function but is not the main luteal negative-feedback hormone.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q016.takeaway: Inhibin selectively suppresses pituitary FSH secretion.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q016.displayText:
Inhibin selectively suppresses pituitary FSH secretion.

The inhibins inhibit FSH secretion by the gonadotrophs of the anterior pituitary (hence the name inhibin) in a classic negative feedback arrangement.
emphasis: Inhibin selectively suppresses pituitary FSH secretion

rationales.a: Inhibin’s primary pituitary action is FSH inhibition, not prolactin suppression.
rationales.b: Estradiol synthesis is not the primary endocrine target of inhibin.
rationales.c: TSH regulation is unrelated to inhibin’s principal action.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q017.takeaway: Inhibin B is released by developing ovarian follicles, especially granulosa cells in the follicular phase.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q017.displayText:
Inhibin B is released by developing ovarian follicles, especially granulosa cells in the follicular phase.

The inhibins are produced by the granulosa cells of the ovarian follicle, as well as other tissues, including the pituitary, the brain, the adrenal gland, the kidney, the bone marrow, the corpus luteum, and the placenta. Inhibin A is produced by the corpus luteum whereas inhibin B is mainly produced by granulosa cells of the follicle.

FSH specifically stimulates the granulosa cells to produce inhibins.

Just before ovulation, after the granulosa cells acquire LH receptors, LH also stimulates the production of inhibin by granulosa cells.
emphasis: Inhibin B is released by developing ovarian follicles, especially granulosa cells in the follicular phase

rationales.b: Ovarian stroma is not the main inhibin B source.
rationales.c: Surface epithelium does not secrete the principal inhibin B pool.
rationales.d: Corpus luteum is more associated with progesterone and inhibin A than the follicular inhibin B source.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q018.takeaway: The corpus luteum is the major progesterone source during a normal nonpregnant luteal phase.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q018.displayText:
The corpus luteum is the major progesterone source during a normal nonpregnant luteal phase.

The source of progesterone during the normal menstrual cycle is corpus luteum.
Progesterone is also secreted by the placenta, and the ovarian follicle (in small amounts).
emphasis: The corpus luteum is the major progesterone source during a normal nonpregnant luteal phase

rationales.b: Ovarian stroma does not produce the cycle’s main postovulatory progesterone.
rationales.c: Ovarian surface epithelium is not steroidogenic source of luteal progesterone.
rationales.d: Anterior pituitary produces gonadotropins, not progesterone.
